title: Socrates behind them all
hook: Stoics, Cynics, Skeptics and Plato's school all looked back to Socrates, in different ways

segments.voice: Yesterday: the skeptics, the painter's sponge, and calm that came when they stopped forcing an answer. Your line was I'm not sure. Where did you say it? Day six hundred fifty-six.

Four siblings sit around a table after a funeral, each telling stories about their father. One remembers how tough he was. One, how little he cared about money. One, how he questioned everything. One, how deep he could go. They're all right, and they barely sound like the same man. That's roughly what happened to Socrates. He wrote nothing. Athens put him to death. And school after school we've met these last weeks claimed him as a father. Today: Socrates behind them all.
screen: `FOUR SIBLINGS, ONE FATHER.` → `HE WROTE NOTHING.` → `SCHOOL AFTER SCHOOL CLAIMED HIM.`

segments.voice: First, the Stoics. Remember Zeno, shipwrecked near Athens? Diogenes Laërtius says he sat in a bookshop reading a book of memories of Socrates by Xenophon, and asked where men like that could be found. The bookseller pointed to Crates walking by. The Stoics took Socrates' conviction that virtue is what really matters, and his calm in the face of death. Second, the Cynics. Their tradition traced itself to Antisthenes, a close companion of Socrates. They took his poverty, his bare feet, his habit of saying hard things in public. Plato is said to have called Diogenes the Cynic a Socrates gone mad. Third, the skeptics, and Plato's own school. In the Academy, Plato's successors eventually took up the Socrates who said he knew nothing, and turned that into a method of doubting. Plato himself made Socrates the main speaker of his dialogues, searching for what justice and courage really are. Fourth, the exception. Epicurus, in his garden, did not claim Socrates, and his followers were often critical of him. So Socrates isn't behind absolutely everyone. But what the others shared was his method: asking. Ask someone what courage is. Listen. Ask again. Find the gap in the answer, including your own. The Greek word for that testing is elenchos. Plato has him say at his trial that a life without this kind of examining isn't worth living. Each school took a different Socrates. All of them kept the question.
screen: `STOICS: ZENO IN THE BOOKSHOP.` · `CYNICS: SOCRATES GONE MAD.` · `ACADEMY: HE KNEW NOTHING.` · `EPICURUS: THE EXCEPTION.` · then, large: `ASK.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Pick one word you use a lot and rarely examine: success, kindness, home, enough. Ask yourself, the Socratic way: what is it? Give your first answer. Then test it. Is there a case where that answer doesn't fit? Adjust. Ask again. You don't need to finish. Just notice how much is folded inside a word you thought you knew. Then think of one person you could ask a real question today, and what it would be. The bell holds the time.
Socrates behind them all. Stoics, Cynics, skeptics and Plato's school each looked back to Socrates, each to a different side of him. Today's word.
Your line: ask. Today, ask one person one real question, the kind where you don't already know the answer, and listen all the way to the end. Day six hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Students of ancient philosophy trace several of the Hellenistic schools back to Socrates, and some still practice his method of questioning a familiar idea until its gaps appear.

fork.reveal: the bookseller pointed to the Cynic Crates, and Zeno followed him. the Stoic porch began with a question about Socrates.

original.note: Greek: testing, cross-examination. The name later given to Socrates' method of questioning.

trapdoor: what you thought: Socrates founded one school of philosophy.
what it means: he founded none and wrote nothing, yet Stoics, Cynics, skeptics and Platonists all claimed a different Socrates.

what a scholar hears: Diogenes Laërtius says Zeno was reading book two of Xenophon's Memorabilia; Epicureans like Colotes attacked Socrates, and the Academic skeptics under Arcesilaus revived his disavowal of knowledge.

sources.work: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: cut the date 399 BC (not in the cited text); Zeno was shipwrecked near Athens (off Piraeus), not in it; 'nearly every school' and 'most of them' softened; trapdoor's unsourced 'often called the Socratic schools' replaced with DL's Memorabilia book-two detail; howItsDone softened.
Zeno reading Xenophon's Memorabilia book 2 in a bookshop, and the bookseller pointing to Crates: DL 7.2–3. Confirm.
Antisthenes as founder-figure of the Cynics: DL 6.1–2 (modern scholars debate the lineage). Hedged 'traced itself'.
'A Socrates gone mad' said of Diogenes by Plato: DL 6.54. Confirm.
Arcesilaus and the skeptical Academy reviving Socratic disavowal of knowledge: Cicero, Academica 1.44–45. Confirm.
Epicurean criticism of Socrates (e.g. Colotes). Confirm.
